skills.name: Problem-solving strategies (2): representing and tracing algorithms

note.text:
Algorithms can be written as:
• pseudocode: short structured English, for example
  INPUT mark
  IF mark ≥ 10 THEN OUTPUT “pass” ELSE OUTPUT “fail”
• a flowchart, with standard symbols: oval (start/end), parallelogram (input/output), rectangle (process), diamond (decision), arrows (flow).
Tracing (dry running) an algorithm means following it step by step with test values to find its output and check it is correct.
Example: “Start with x = 3. Repeat 4 times: add 5 to x. Output x.” gives 3 + 4 × 5 = 23.
Test with normal values and boundary values (exactly 10 in the pass/fail example).

worked_example.problem: Trace: “Start with x = {x}. Repeat {n} times: add {b} to x. Output x.”

cards.idea: Flowchart symbols: oval, parallelogram, rectangle, diamond, arrows.
example: A diamond asks a yes/no question.

cards.idea: Tracing means following the algorithm step by step with test values.
example: Start {x}, add {b} three times: {traceAdd(x, b, three)}.

cards.idea: A decision chooses a path: IF … THEN … ELSE.

check.prompt: INPUT mark. IF mark ≥ {p} THEN OUTPUT “pass” ELSE OUTPUT “fail”. What is output when mark = {m}?

misconceptions.explain: Compare carefully: {m} ≥ {p} is {m >= p ? 'true' : 'false'} (equal counts as ≥).

questions.prompt: Match each flowchart symbol to its meaning.

misconceptions.explain: The step is repeated {n} times, not once.

misconceptions.explain: Doubling multiplies by {two} each time; it does not add.
